newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Angola ready to inaugurate new unity government. [CORRECTED 14:43 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Angola ready to inaugurate new unity government. [CORRECTED 14:43 GMT]

text.p: Angola's government and the former rebel movement UNITA, who fought each other for 20 years, are near the end of a bumpy road to full reconciliation when they inaugurate a power-sharing unity government on Friday.

The country's parliament on Tuesday cleared away the final hurdle in the fragile peace process, which began with a treaty in November 1994, by rushing through a bill giving UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi special status.
"We can see no reasons to prevent the new government being formed on Friday," said UNITA representative Isaias Samakuva.

Parliamentary deputies of UNITA's old foes in the ruling MPLA put aside their misgivings to vote overwhelmingly for the statute. "It's a bad law, but we've passed it out of political necessity," one government minister said.

The legislation, which formally makes Savimbi president of the largest opposition party and gives him, among other things, the right to regular consultation with the national president and an official residence in Luanda, can only be amended with his consent.
UNITA, which went to war against the MPLA on independence from Portugal in 1975, had threatened to boycott the scheduled swearing-in of their 70 deputies if the law was not passed.

The deputies, who won their parliamentary seats in the aborted elections of 1992, were sworn in on Wednesday (corrects from 'are due to be sworn in on Thursday'). The movement will take four ministerial posts as well as several vice-ministerial offices and provincial governorships.

The capital Luanda has started preparing for an influx of foreign heads of state, including South Africa's Nelson Mandela, with truckloads of heavily armed riot police roaming the streets. The parliamentary building is hurriedly being repainted.

The United Nations, which has started a gradual withdrawal of the 6,000-strong UNAVEM peacekeeping force, argues that the inauguration of the unity government would be a crucial step in implementation of the 1994 Lusaka Protocol.
Political analysts are divided over the significance of the new government and to what extent it can consolidate peace in Angola.
"It's a confidence-building step and it sends the right message to the international community," one Western diplomat said.

He said most international donors, including the International Monetary Fund, had released millions of dollars pledged for reconstructing Angola, which had been promised on condition the new government was formed.
Other diplomats argued, however, that many problems still needed to be resolved before peace in Angola was really secure.
"This is the beginning, not the end," said one, adding that UNITA remained in control of most of Angola's territory and still had the capacity to return to war.

He also pointed out that despite his new status, Savimbi had said he would not be travelling to Luanda to participate in Friday's ceremonies because the security situation was still not stable enough to enable him to leave his headquarters in Angola's central highlands.
